notes:
- Your email signature belongs to an address now, not to the whole agent. On an agent your team
  shares, a reply written from a colleague's own address went out over the owner's name, and the
  one person who could see that happening was the client reading it. Every address is signed with
  its own signature. An address that has none is signed with the name of whoever it belongs to.
- A signature can be a picture. Put a logo beside the words, or use an image that is the whole
  signature with the name, title and phone drawn into it. You pick small, medium or large, and the
  preview is drawn at the size that goes out rather than as a thumbnail, so you find out it is too
  big before a client does.
- Somebody who is not the owner can set their own signature by telling the agent in chat. The
  Archie window belongs to the owner, so until now the owner was typing everybody's signature.
- A draft can wait for a time you pick. Every draft your agent hands you has a Send later button
  offering an hour from now, three hours, or the next morning, each printed as the time it actually
  comes to. If the other person writes back on that thread before it goes, the queued reply stops
  itself and hands the draft back to you with a line at the top saying why. Nothing leaves your
  account unless you send it or set the time for it yourself.
- Your agent can start an email, not only answer one. "Send Sam an email saying let's get lunch"
  used to come back as an explanation of why it could only reply to mail already in your inbox.
- Campaign Watch is new. It reads your lemlist campaigns and tells you who wrote back, what they
  said, and which campaign has quietly stopped working. It writes the replies and you send them.
- On a shared agent, somebody who is not the owner can answer mail sent to their own address. Every
  mail action counted as acting on the owner's accounts, so the only way to let a colleague reply to
  their own client was to hand them the owner's mailbox as well.
- A calendar can now be shared while the mail on the same account stays private. Sharing somebody's
  working hours, which is what colleagues need from each other all day, used to mean sharing their
  inbox too.
- Connected apps say whose they are: one person's, or the whole business's. There was one key per
  service, so "add that to my list" meant the owner's list wherever the person asking sat.
- Meeting notes accounts are one per person as well. Pasting a second Fireflies key used to replace
  the first with nothing on screen to say so, and whoever pasted last was the only person whose
  meetings the agent could see.
- The owner can read what the agent has said to everybody else on the roster, on the agent's page.
  Every conversation but the owner's own happened somewhere the owner could not see. It is read
  only, with no box to type into: answering in somebody else's chat would put the owner's words in
  a room the owner is not in.
- Everything you reach with a pasted key is one list on the Connections tab, under Apps. Meeting
  recorders had a tab of their own and GoHighLevel had no place on the tab at all, so connecting a
  CRM meant going and finding the add-on that wanted one.
- Reconnect opens inside the row you pressed it on. It used to open a panel at the top of the list,
  so pressing Reconnect on the fourth mailbox opened something over the first one, and the only way
  to tell what you had pressed was to read the address in the heading.
- A connection that nothing installed can use now says so, with an amber dot on the Connections tab
  and on the sidebar beside it. The add-ons that would use it are buttons you can press right
  there, instead of a trip to the store to look up what you have just been told.
- Fireflies, lemlist and GoHighLevel have their own logos in the list. They wore two-letter
  monograms beside twenty real logos, which read as three services that had failed to load.
- Response quality now reaches the part of your agent that reads mail and texts in the background.
  That part was pinned to the middle setting whatever you had chosen, so somebody who moved the dial
  to Economy to spend less went on paying the middle price on every message that arrived, and no
  screen said so. Deciding what a message is amounts to sorting the mail, and sorting is what the
  cheaper settings are for.
- There is a second number beside "Tell me about at most", called "Read at most". The first one is
  about your attention. The second is about your money, because working out what a message is costs
  a little whether or not it turns out to be worth telling you about, and nothing counted that
  before. Neither one ever holds up a Draft button you pressed yourself.
- The Spending screen can name what used to land in "Everything else", which was about half of
  every call your agent made. A row called everything else is only useful when it is the small one.
- Your agent pays less to read the same mail. A reply carries every earlier message in the thread
  underneath it, and your agent was being handed all of it every time. The quoted part comes off
  first now, so what it reads is the message somebody actually just sent.
- Routines that come due in the same minute run one after another instead of all at once, which
  makes every one after the first cheaper.
- The chat says what a model sounds like when it is wrong, under the box rather than in the
  transcript. Being right and being wrong sound identical coming out of one: no hedge, no
  hesitation, nothing in the words to go on.
- Fixed: Response quality had quietly stopped existing for every add-on installed from the store.
  It survived only on skills you write yourself, so a setting the app describes in three places was
  adjustable on almost nothing.
- Fixed: an Outlook mailbox could report itself as broken when it was only busy. Outlook allows one
  app four requests against a mailbox at a time, and a twenty-message list went out as twenty at
  once, so the mailbox refused and your agent handed you the refusal as an account problem and
  named the address, which invited you to reconnect something that was never broken.
- Fixed: an add-on that names the one service it needs was handed every key on your agent instead
  of that one. An add-on that names nothing still reaches everything, which is what an add-on you
  write yourself does.
- Fixed: starting a new agent from an existing one copied connections belonging to somebody who is
  not on the new agent, which left keys nobody there could use.
- Fixed: the remove button could fall off the end of a mailbox row.
- Fixed: on Windows, the video add-ons downloaded an old copy of one of the tools they need, so
  they did not run.
- Fixed: on Windows, setting up phone access rebuilt everything every time it checked, because it
  could not tell that nothing had changed since the last check.

- Your agent can tell you about mail it is not going to answer. Email Manager has a new setting for
  what reaches you: only mail that needs a reply, which is what it did before and is still what a
  new install does; anything a real person wrote; or everything your ignore list did not drop.
  Until now, mail your agent decided needed no reply was dropped without a word, so a decision that
  went wrong looked exactly like an agent that had stopped working.
- Email Replies is now called Email Manager. Answering is one of the three things it does, beside
  watching what arrives and filing it away, alongside answering.
- Its settings are in six named groups instead of one long column, and every on-off setting is a
  switch at the end of its row instead of a tick box.
- An email your agent is not handing you a draft for now gets two or three sentences instead of one
  line, and they carry the date, amount or deadline that was in the message.
- Your ignore list and the limit on how many messages an hour your agent sends you are visible even
  when automatic drafts are off. Both were being applied the whole time, from boxes you could not
  see.
- Times your agent writes for somebody else say which zone they are in. A reply offering "9am" left
  the person reading it to work out whether that meant your morning or theirs.
- Installing an add-on no longer asks you something you have already told this agent. An answer you
  gave once is filled in for the next add-on that asks the same question.
- You can stop one agent reading the web. On that agent's page, under Response quality, "Don't let
  this agent read the web" turns off opening pages and searching, for that agent and for every
  skill you install later. Email, calendar and chat keep working, and so do the services you
  connected yourself on the Connections tab. Worth turning on if the computer running Archie
  belongs to your work.
- Fixed: every question you asked about an Outlook mailbox failed before it left Archie. Asking
  whether a message had arrived from somebody sent Outlook a request in a shape it rejects, and
  your agent then reported the mailbox as unreadable and named the address, which invited you to
  reconnect an account that was never broken. Watching an Outlook inbox was never affected, which
  is how both could be true on the same account at the same time.
- Fixed: the list of who can message your agent could show a stranger's phone number under your own
  name. A Telegram account id is ten digits, the same shape as a phone number here, so it was drawn
  as one. The number was real, and it belonged to somebody who has never heard of Archie.
- Fixed: your agent could be watching no inboxes at all while the panel said it was on. If you had
  chosen which inboxes to watch and later reconnected those accounts, the saved choice pointed at
  accounts that no longer existed. It watches all of them now, and says so.
- The Activity log, on the agent's Setup tab, now says what your email watching is actually doing:
  which inboxes it is watching, when it is taking its first look at a mailbox and holding back
  everything already sitting in there, and when it has lost track of one. The first look is what
  catches people out. Send yourself a test message before it happens and that message is already
  behind, so nothing arrives and nothing is wrong.
- Fixed: pressing Draft on an email your agent had decided needed no reply did nothing at all. It
  asked itself the same question again and got the same answer. Pressing Draft is your decision, so
  it writes the draft now.
- Fixed: Text Replies could go quiet with nothing wrong. A sign-in that had expired, or a dropped
  connection, looked exactly like a text that needed no answer.
- Fixed: a summary sent to Telegram could arrive with stray underscores through it, once summaries
  became long enough to run to a second line.
- Fixed: replacing the token for a chat app your agent is already on emptied the list of who is
  allowed to message it, and the screen said the opposite. It now names who would have to claim the
  agent again, before you press save, and sends you to the claim code afterward.
- Fixed: a question about what was said on a past call could be handed to your calendar instead of
  to the add-on that reads call transcripts.
- Fixed: the video skills could not run on any computer that downloaded their tools rather than
  building them, which is every computer but a developer's. Video Synthesizer works again.

- Your agent now says when it cannot read a mailbox, instead of looking healthy and going quiet.
  A sign-in that has lapsed, or a permission your workplace withdrew, turns the agent's status to
  "Needs attention" and names the address, what the mail provider said, and where to press
  Reconnect.
- Your agent also says when it wrote a reply and could not deliver it. A bot removed from a group,
  or one whose permission to post was taken away, used to look exactly like an agent with nothing
  to say.
- Every connected email account has a Reconnect button now, not only the ones that could be given
  more access. An account that had stopped working looked perfect and had nothing to press, and the
  only way back was to remove it and add it again, which no screen said.
- Fixed: connecting a calendar from inside a skill took away that account's email. It asked for
  calendar permission alone, and Outlook and Gmail both hand back exactly what was asked for, so
  everything else was dropped. It now asks for what the account already had as well.
- Fixed: your agent could stop reading email entirely after you reconnected an account. Reconnecting
  changed the account's identity behind the scenes, so the list of inboxes to watch pointed at
  nothing, and the watcher ran every five minutes on no inboxes at all while the panel said it was
  on.
- Fixed, on a shared agent: reconnecting a mailbox that belonged to one person handed it back to
  everybody, so their mail started arriving in the conversation the team shares.
- Fixed: a saved thing named with an accent, like a subscription called "Uber" with the umlaut,
  could stop all email checking until Archie was restarted. Nothing was shown when it happened.
- Fixed: the chat inside Archie could show a green Live badge and refuse every message you typed,
  after the agent restarted itself. It now keeps working, and an agent that stops on its own says
  so instead of claiming to be running.
- Fixed: removing a Google account from an agent that also had Outlook could break Google Tasks
  days later, with nothing connecting the two.
- Fixed: removing the last inbox you had chosen to watch started watching all of them, including
  other people's on a shared agent.
- Fixed: a light whose bridge no longer accepted Archie's key was reported as a missing light, so
  you went looking for a lamp that was exactly where you left it.
- Fixed: learning your writing style from your sent mail could, over the following weeks, run an
  Outlook sign-in down until it stopped working.

- A mailbox your agent could not read is now reported as exactly that, with what the mail provider
  said about it. An expired sign-in, a permission a workplace withdrew, or Outlook having a bad
  minute all used to arrive looking identical to a quiet morning: "the inbox is empty".
- Connecting an email account opens the mailbox once, straight away, while you are still sitting
  there. If it will not open, nothing is connected and the screen says what the provider said,
  instead of leaving a green row that never works.
- Your agent no longer insists it can read a mailbox that has never once opened. It used to be told
  to say it had access on the strength of the permissions alone, so it argued with people whose
  mail it genuinely could not reach.
- An Outlook account at a company or school whose administrator has to approve Archie now names the
  setting to ask for, spelled the way their admin console spells it, and where it lives. Asking an
  IT department to "approve an app called Archie" gets a reply asking which permission and where.
- The calendar is offered whichever email you use. That button was tied to Google being configured,
  so somebody connecting Outlook was never offered a calendar at all.
- Searching the store for "outlook" finds the email and calendar add-ons. Every one of them names
  both providers now, and Email Manager and Calendar answer to "outlook" spoken aloud as well.
- The store says which add-ons need an AI account of your own on the row, before you press Install,
  rather than refusing after you have pressed it.
- Two guides that did not exist. One is how to update Archie. The other is connecting your email and
  calendar: where the button is, what each permission lets your agent do, what to send a workplace
  administrator when it refuses, and what to do when an account stops working.
- The first-run screens say what Archie needs to run: this computer left awake and plugged into
  power, with the sleep setting named and where to change it, and a cable from your router if you
  can reach one. A routine set for 7:30am needs this computer awake at 7:30am.
- "Needs attention" is a button. It was two words beside a small icon whose only explanation was a
  tooltip, so there was nothing to press and, on a touchscreen, nothing to read.
- Six screens sent you to Settings to connect an email or calendar account. That is not where it
  is. They name the Connections tab, the section inside it, and the button, and they say to tick
  the permissions before you sign in.
- Fixed: an error that said only that something had failed now says where to go and what to press.
  A refused key names the screen you paste it into; a lost connection names the cable to check.
- Fixed: running out of credit on your own AI account names that company and its billing page. It
  used to send you to a company you may not have an account with.

- Reminders arrive with something to do about them. Done ticks the matching task off your list,
  Later offers an hour from now, this evening or tomorrow morning, and Dismiss closes it. Answering
  in words still works: say "did that" or "move it to four" and the buttons settle themselves.
- Ask to be reminded and you get a reminder. It used to write a task instead, which is a row you
  have to go and look at and interrupts nobody. Now it sets the reminder, adds the task where the
  thing is also work worth writing down, and tells you it did both.
- Cancel a reminder by what it is about ("cancel the invoice one") rather than by a number you were
  never shown. The task it was filed with goes with it.
- Archie can move to another computer. Account has a Moving and backups section that writes one
  file holding every agent: their instructions, their skills with the answers you gave, routines
  with their schedules, records, memory and chat history. Nothing in it stores a location, so the
  same file works from a Mac to a Windows PC. No passwords or tokens travel, on purpose, and the
  file tells you what you will be reconnecting.
- A connected account that nothing is using now says so, and names the add-ons that would use it.
  Connecting your email and getting nothing out of it was invisible before.
- Every setup that ends in a long code now begins by saying where to stand. Telegram gets a step of
  its own, because reading a 46-character token off a phone and typing it into a laptop is the part
  that goes wrong. Addresses inside a step are links now, instead of something to retype while you
  are already holding two devices.
- Archie for Business: you pick the departments a company needs and its agents arrive set up for
  them, instead of building each one. Agents are peers, with no head agent above them, and the
  company page shows who does what.
- Archie for Business: a list belongs to the company rather than to whichever agent wrote it, so
  one department can hand another a list without handing over everything else it keeps.
- Fixed, on Outlook: a reply would not send unless you had also allowed Archie to file mail. It
  sends either way now. The permission itself is named for what it does, because it decides both
  filing and whether a reply lands inside the conversation it answers, and it only ever said
  filing.
- Fixed, on Outlook: an account at a company or school whose administrator has to approve Archie
  now says so, and says what to ask for. It used to say "try again and choose Accept" about a
  screen with no Accept on it.
- Fixed: the Chat tab could open blank until you reloaded the window.
- Fixed: a task list saved by an earlier version was invisible to the agent that kept it, which
  then said its tools were not working.
- Fixed: your agent sometimes answered "I processed the request but couldn't generate a response".
- Fixed: a moment of bad network was reported as a failure and left you to send the message again.
- Fixed: the AI account panel showed Claude selected while saying OpenAI was connected.
- Fixed: the strip above the message box showed the raw asterisks and link addresses of the message
  you were replying to.

- Your new agent asks what your days look like, then sets itself up from the answers. The skills
  and routines that fit your work are chosen and switched on while you are still talking to it,
  and it tells you what it added.
- Its page opens on what arrived: each ability named, with what it does, and how to take any of
  them back off.
- You can tell your agent to remove a skill or pause a routine and it does it, after one tap to
  confirm. Pausing keeps the routine and everything you set on it.
- Waiting On follows up across texts as well as email. Ask by email, get the answer as a text,
  and it still closes the loop. On a Mac, with the text watch on.
- Archie for Business asks about the business: what it does, who its customers are, and who else
  will be talking to it. It no longer asks a company owner their age.
- Fixed: a new agent said hello twice, and then asked your name after greeting you by it.
- Fixed: confirmations for adding or removing an add-on are tappable now, instead of asking you
  to type the word back.
- Fixed: deleting an agent showed an error after the agent was already gone.
- Fixed: the welcome cards played after every new agent instead of only the first.

- You can try Archie before paying for it. A new account gets free credits that run an agent on
  our AI account, or fourteen days on an AI account of your own.
- Your agent answers on iMessage, on a Mac. That makes six chat apps, alongside Telegram,
  Discord, Slack, Signal and Matrix.
- You can talk to your agent in Archie's own window. It is one conversation, so a question you
  start in your chat app can be finished here.
- Send it a photo and it looks at the photo. It can make pictures too. Send a voice note instead
  of typing, and have replies read out loud.
- Your agent can use a website itself, the same way you would, when there is no direct
  connection to it.
- Outlook and Microsoft calendars work the way Google's do. Sign in once and your agent can read
  the mail and the diary.
- "Remind me to pay the water bill tomorrow at 10am" now sets a reminder.
- Your agent can learn how you write from what you have already sent, and draft in your voice.
- The store has shelves, packs and a cart, so a set of add-ons installs in one go.
- Archie has a face. Ember is the app's own character, and every agent gets its own version of
  him.
- Dark mode is stone rather than brown, and every color in the app was measured against its
  background so nothing is left faint.
- On Windows: the media tools (transcription, video) install on Windows now, and this is the
  first version Windows can update itself from.
- Fixed: sixteen routines woke up every morning to work out whether it was their day. They run
  on the day they mean now.
- Fixed: a restart could overwrite your agent's first message, and a long reply stopped one
  message short of the bottom of the window.
